name: slots.courseSpecifics
description: The students are Norwegian upper-secondary students in Vg3 who have chosen English 2 as a programme subject; it builds on English 1. English is their second language and most have Norwegian as their first. Work in English at an advanced, academic level, and when an error comes from Norwegian, name the contrast briefly. Expect independent reflection: ask for the student's own position and the reasons for it, not a textbook answer. When a fact, date or institution matters, keep to established facts, and say so when something has changed recently or is disputed. The course gives one written and one oral grade for coursework, and a student can be drawn for a centrally set written exam of five hours with no preparation day, or for a locally set oral exam.

name: Choose strategies for reading, listening, speaking and writing
description: choose strategies that suit the situation and purpose, such as reading a scholarly article selectively, taking structured notes from a lecture, planning a long text before drafting, and paraphrasing when a word is missing in speech.

name: Write with precision and variety
description: choose the precise word over the approximate one, and vary vocabulary and sentence structure so that a long text stays exact and readable.

name: Tone
description: Tone: the attitude a text expresses towards its subject and its reader, such as neutral, ironic, urgent or sympathetic.

name: Control the tone of your text
description: keep a tone that suits the purpose and audience through a whole text, and identify and describe the tone of someone else's text.

name: Cut wordiness
description: cut empty phrases such as "it is important to note that", repetition and needless nominalisations, without losing content.

name: Academic stance
description: Academic stance: the writer's position towards claims and sources, signalled by evaluative words such as convincingly and questionable, by reporting verbs and by hedging, rather than by "I think".

name: Reporting verbs
description:
argue: put forward a claim with reasons
claim: state something that may be disputed
suggest: put forward tentatively
emphasise: give special importance to
acknowledge: accept that something is true or valid
concede: admit, often reluctantly, that the other side has a point
dispute: say that something is wrong
maintain: keep insisting that something is true

name: Show your stance towards sources
description: show your own position towards the sources you use, by choosing reporting verbs and evaluative words that signal whether you agree with, doubt or reject a claim.

name: Structures for emphasis
description:
Cleft sentence: a sentence split in two to emphasise one part, as in "It was the war that changed everything."
Inversion: putting the verb before the subject after a negative or limiting opening, as in "Never before had the party lost so heavily."
Participle clause: a clause built on an -ing or -ed form instead of a full verb, as in "Having lost the election, the party changed its leader."

name: Use structures for emphasis and variety
description: use cleft sentences, inversion and participle clauses for emphasis and variety, and avoid participle clauses whose implied subject does not match the main clause.

name: Revise your own text for style
description: revise a text of your own for precision, tone, concision and variety, and explain what each change improves.

name: Premise, conclusion and assumption
description:
Premise: a statement given as a reason.
Conclusion: what the premises are meant to support.
Assumption: an unstated premise that the argument relies on.

name: Reconstruct an argument
description: set out the argument of a text as premises and conclusion, including the unstated assumptions it relies on.

name: Logical fallacy
description: Logical fallacy: a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument seem stronger than it is.

name: Common fallacies
description:
straw man: attacking a distorted version of the opponent's argument
ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the argument
false dilemma: presenting only two options when there are more
slippery slope: claiming that one step will inevitably lead to an extreme outcome
appeal to authority: treating a claim as true because an authority said it, often outside their field
hasty generalisation: drawing a general conclusion from too few cases
whataboutism: answering criticism by pointing to someone else's wrongdoing
post hoc: assuming that because B followed A, A caused B

name: Spot fallacies in a debate
description: identify fallacies in a speech, debate or opinion piece, and explain why each one does not support the conclusion.

name: Correlation and causation
description:
Correlation: two things tend to vary together.
Causation: one thing actually brings about the other; a correlation alone does not show this.

name: Judge whether the evidence holds
description: judge whether the evidence in a text supports its claim: how many cases there are, how representative they are, whether a correlation is presented as a cause, and what is missing.

name: Assess the strength of an argument
description: assess the overall strength of an argument by weighing its reasoning, its evidence and its assumptions, and say what would make it stronger.

name: Perspective
description: Perspective: the position from which something is seen, shaped by such things as nationality, class, gender, ethnicity, politics and time.

name: Read a text from another perspective
description: read a text critically from a perspective other than the one it invites, asking whose voices are heard, whose are missing and whose interests it serves.

name: Reflect independently on a text
description: discuss a text with independent reflection: form and justify your own view of it instead of repeating the text's view or a standard reading, and change your view when the arguments call for it.

name: Scholarly and popular sources
description:
Scholarly source: a text written by researchers for other researchers, with references, such as a journal article or academic book.
Peer review: checking of a scholarly text by other experts in the field before it is published.
Popular source: a text written for a general audience, such as a newspaper article or a blog.

name: Search for scholarly sources
description: search databases and library catalogues for scholarly sources, such as Google Scholar or Oria, and narrow the search with keywords, synonyms and filters.

name: Evaluate a source for an academic text
description: evaluate how reliable and relevant a source is for an academic text, considering who wrote it, for what purpose, when, what evidence it builds on, and whether it is peer-reviewed or confirmed by others.

name: Integrate and cite sources consistently
description: integrate quotations and paraphrases with signal phrases, and cite each in the text and in a reference list in one citation style, such as APA, consistently.

name: Synthesise several sources
description: combine several sources in one paragraph, showing where they agree and disagree, rather than presenting them one at a time.

name: Academic integrity
description:
Plagiarism: presenting someone else's words or ideas, including text produced by an AI tool, as your own.
Academic integrity: being honest about where every word, idea and piece of data in your text comes from, including how you have used AI tools.

name: Use AI tools honestly in research
description: use AI tools in research honestly: check every fact and reference they give against a real source, never cite a source you have not seen, and state how you used them where that is required.

name: Types of academic text
description:
Research essay: a text that answers a research question using several sources.
Comparative essay: a text that examines two subjects side by side to reach a conclusion about both.
Literary essay: a text that argues for an interpretation of one or more literary works.

name: Write a nuanced thesis
description: write a thesis statement that takes a clear and nuanced position and indicates how the text will develop it.

name: Structure a long academic text
description: plan and structure a long academic text with a logical order of sections, headings where they help, and transitions that show how each part moves the argument on.

name: Answer the strongest objection
description: present the strongest objection to your claim fairly, and answer it by conceding, refuting or qualifying your claim.

name: Write a comparative essay
description: write a comparative essay organised point by point rather than one subject at a time, ending in a conclusion about what the comparison shows.

name: Write a research essay
description: write a research essay that answers a research question with several sources, synthesising them, answering objections and reaching a supported conclusion.

name: Give an academic presentation
description: give an academic presentation with a clear thesis or research question, signposting, references to sources and a conclusion, and keep to the time.

name: Defend your views under questioning
description: answer questions after a presentation or in an oral exam: clarify, defend your view with evidence, and admit the limits of what you know.

name: Take part in a seminar discussion
description: take part in or lead a seminar discussion of a text: bring prepared questions, build on others' points, and sum up where the group agrees and disagrees.

name: Literary period
description: Literary period: a span of time whose literature shares themes, forms and ideas shaped by its history and society; the borders between periods are approximate.

name: Literary periods in English
description:
the English Renaissance: about 1500–1660
Romanticism: about 1790–1830
the Victorian period: 1837–1901
Modernism: about 1900–1940
the Harlem Renaissance: the 1920s and 1930s
postcolonial literature: from about 1950
postmodernism: from about 1960

description:

Pride and Prejudice (1813): Jane Austen

The Great Gatsby (1925): F. Scott Fitzgerald

Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937): Zora Neale Hurston
Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949): George Orwell

To Kill a Mockingbird (1960): Harper Lee

name: Shakespearean drama
description:
Tragedy: a play in which the hero's flaw or error leads to their downfall.
Soliloquy: a speech in which a character speaks their thoughts alone on stage.
Blank verse: unrhymed lines in iambic pentameter, used for much of Shakespeare's dialogue.

name: Romanticism
description: Romanticism: a movement that reacted against the Enlightenment's stress on reason and against industrialisation, and valued feeling, imagination, nature and the individual.

name: Victorian realism
description: Victorian realism: novels that portray society in detail, often criticising class divisions, poverty and the effects of industrialisation, as Dickens does.

name: Modernism
description:
Modernism: a movement after about 1900 that broke with traditional forms to express a fragmented, uncertain world, especially after the First World War.
Stream of consciousness: a technique that renders a character's flow of thoughts and impressions as they occur.

name: Harlem Renaissance
description: Harlem Renaissance: a flowering of African American literature, music and art centred on Harlem in New York in the 1920s and 1930s, exploring Black identity and experience.

name: The American Dream
description: American Dream: the idea that anyone in the USA can achieve success and a better life through hard work, whatever their background; an idea literature often questions.

name: Postcolonial literature
description: Postcolonial literature: literature from or about former colonies that deals with colonialism and its after-effects, such as identity, language, power and the voices of the colonised.

name: Postmodernism
description:
Postmodernism: a movement from about the 1960s that questions grand narratives and fixed truths, often through irony, mixed genres and play with form.
Metafiction: fiction that draws attention to itself as fiction.

name: Historical and cultural context
description:
Historical context: the events, conditions and ideas of the time a text was written in or is set in.
Cultural context: the values, beliefs and traditions that shape a text and its readers.

name: Place a text in its literary period
description: place a text in its literary period, and point out features of form and theme typical of that period.

name: Interpret a passage from Shakespeare
description: read and interpret a passage from a Shakespeare play, using a modern paraphrase as support, and explain what it shows about character and theme.

name: Interpret a text in its context
description: interpret a literary text in light of its historical and cultural context, showing how the context sheds light on the text without reducing the text to it.

name: Interpret a poem from an earlier period
description: interpret a poem from an earlier period, such as a Romantic poem, and explain how it reflects the ideas of its time.

name: Interpret a modernist text
description: interpret a modernist text, explaining how its form, such as stream of consciousness or a fragmented structure, expresses its view of the world.

name: Read a text with a postcolonial lens
description: read a text with a postcolonial lens: whose perspective it takes, how colonisers and colonised are portrayed, and what language and identity mean in it.

name: Discuss the American Dream in a text
description: discuss how a novel, short story or film treats the American Dream, drawing on the text and its context.

name: Compare texts from different periods
description: compare how two texts from different periods treat the same theme, and explain the differences through their contexts.

name: Discuss a literary text
description: discuss a literary text: argue for your interpretation, consider other readings, and assess what the text says to readers today.

name: Write a literary essay with context
description: write a literary essay that interprets one or more texts in their historical and cultural context, with quotations and secondary sources as evidence.

name: British Empire
description: British Empire: the colonies, dominions and other territories ruled by Britain, at its largest in the early twentieth century, when it covered about a quarter of the world's land.

name: Decolonisation
description: Decolonisation: the process, mainly after 1945, by which colonies gained independence, as India did in 1947.

name: Commonwealth of Nations
description: Commonwealth of Nations: a voluntary association of independent states, most of them former British territories, that cooperate on shared values and have the British monarch as their symbolic head.

name: Dates in the history of the British Empire
description:
First Fleet arrives in Australia: 1788
Treaty of Waitangi in New Zealand: 1840
Canadian Confederation: 1867
Irish Free State established: 1922
independence of India and Pakistan: 1947
independence of Ghana: 1957
Hong Kong handed over to China: 1997

name: Soft power and hard power
description:
Soft power: a country's ability to influence others through attraction, such as its culture, values and institutions.
Hard power: influence through military force or economic pressure.

name: Superpower and the Cold War
description:
Superpower: a state with dominant global military, economic and political power, as the USA has been since 1945 and the Soviet Union was until 1991.
Cold War: the rivalry between the USA and the Soviet Union from about 1947 to 1991, fought through arms races, alliances and proxy wars rather than direct war between them.

name: The USA and the UK in international institutions
description:
the United Nations founded: 1945
the Marshall Plan for rebuilding Western Europe: 1948
NATO founded: 1949
the dissolution of the Soviet Union: 1991
permanent members of the UN Security Council: the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China

name: Americanisation and cultural imperialism
description:
Americanisation: the spread of American culture, products and habits to other countries.
Cultural imperialism: the view that a powerful country's culture spreads at the expense of local cultures.

name: Explain the legacy of the British Empire
description: explain how the British Empire spread the English language, legal systems and institutions, and discuss its legacy in former colonies today.

name: Explain the global power of the USA
description: explain how the USA gained global political influence after 1945, through alliances, international institutions and the Cold War, and give examples of how it has used that influence.

name: Analyse cultural influence
description: analyse the cultural influence of an English-speaking country through film, music, the internet or sport, and discuss whether it is enrichment or cultural imperialism.

name: Explain how power made English dominant
description: explain how political and economic power made English dominant in areas such as diplomacy, science and business, and what this means for speakers of other languages.

name: Discuss the influence of English-speaking countries
description: discuss the combined linguistic, cultural and political influence of one or more English-speaking countries on the world, including on Norway, and reach a view of your own.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: The British political system
description:
Constitutional monarchy: a system where the monarch is head of state but has almost no political power.
Parliamentary system: the government is formed from, and answers to, the elected parliament; the Prime Minister leads the party that commands a majority in the House of Commons.
Uncodified constitution: a constitution not written in one single document, but made up of laws, court rulings and conventions.
Devolution: the transfer of some powers from the UK Parliament to elected bodies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: The American political system
description:
Presidential system: the President, who is both head of state and head of government, is elected separately from Congress and does not answer to it.
Separation of powers: legislative power lies with Congress, executive power with the President and judicial power with the courts.
Checks and balances: the ways each branch can limit the others, such as the presidential veto and the Supreme Court's power to strike down laws.
Federalism: the sharing of power between the federal government and the states.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Electoral systems
description:
First past the post: in each constituency the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority; used for the House of Commons and in most US elections.
Electoral College: the system by which the US states choose the President, where in most states the winner of the popular vote takes all the state's electors.
Two-party system: a system dominated by two large parties, which first past the post tends to produce.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Institutions in the UK and the USA
description:
UK Parliament: the House of Commons and the House of Lords
members of the House of Commons: 650
longest time between UK general elections: five years
US Congress: the Senate and the House of Representatives
US Senate: 100 senators, two per state, elected for six years
US House of Representatives: 435 members, elected for two years
US President: elected for four years, at most two terms
US Supreme Court: nine justices, appointed for life
Electoral College: 538 electors, 270 needed to win

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Main political parties
description:
Conservative Party (UK): centre-right
Labour Party (UK): centre-left
Liberal Democrats (UK): centrist and liberal
Scottish National Party: for Scottish independence
Reform UK: right-wing populist
Republican Party (US): conservative, right of centre
Democratic Party (US): liberal, left of centre

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Welfare and health care models
description:
Welfare state: a system where the state provides services such as health care to everyone, funded by taxes, as with the NHS in the UK.
Market-based model: a system where health care is mainly paid for through private insurance, as in much of the USA, with public programmes such as Medicare and Medicaid for some groups.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Segregation and the civil rights movement
description:
Segregation: the separation of people by race in schools, transport and public places, legal in the US South under the Jim Crow laws.
Civil rights movement: the movement, especially in the 1950s and 1960s, for equal rights for African Americans and an end to segregation.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Windrush generation
description: Windrush generation: people who came from Caribbean countries to settle in Britain in the decades after 1948, many of whom were later wrongly treated as illegal immigrants in the Windrush scandal that came to light in 2018.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Class and social mobility
description:
Class: a social group defined by such things as background, education, occupation and wealth, in Britain often also marked by accent.
Social mobility: the ability to move to a different class than the one you were born into.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Explain how the UK is governed
description: explain how the UK is governed: how a government is formed, the roles of Parliament, the Prime Minister and the monarch, and what devolution means for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Explain how the USA is governed
description: explain how the USA is governed: the roles of Congress, the President and the Supreme Court, how they check each other, and how power is shared with the states.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Compare the political systems
description: compare the political systems of the UK and the USA, and explain the differences through their history: a monarchy that gradually handed power to parliament, and a republic founded in revolution.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Compare welfare and health care
description: compare health care and welfare in the UK and the USA, and explain the differences through history and political values.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Compare race relations
description: compare the history and present state of race relations in the UK and the USA, from slavery and empire to today's debates.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Trace a current issue back to its history
description: explain how a current social or political issue in an English-speaking country has its roots in history, such as Scottish independence and the union of 1707, or gun rights and the founding of the USA.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Analyse a political speech
description: analyse a political speech from the UK or the USA: its situation and purpose, its argument and rhetoric, and how it draws on the country's history and values.

topic: The UK and the USA compared
name: Convey a comparison of two countries
description: convey a comparison of a social or political issue in two English-speaking countries to an audience, in speech or writing, making the historical background clear and drawing a conclusion of your own.

name: Research question
description: Research question: a precise, open question that a project sets out to answer, narrow enough to be answered with the time and sources available.

name: Narrow a topic to a research question
description: choose a topic from English 2 and narrow it to a research question that can be answered with the sources available.

name: Plan an in-depth project
description: plan an in-depth project: set a timeline, decide which kinds of sources to search, and record notes and references as you go.

name: Present an in-depth project
description: present the findings of your in-depth project orally or in writing, using English sources critically, and say where the sources disagree and what remains uncertain.
